title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target; accordingly, the preregistered confirmatory large‑effect hypothesis (H1) is not testable on the observed data and we report descriptive/conditional inferential results anchored to archived artifacts. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Translating operator intent into device configuration is a central NetOps activity. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as intent→configuration translators that can accelerate operations, but probabilistic generation risks misordered steps, omission of required commands, and other unsafe outputs. Prior work advocates generate→verify→repair patterns that pair probabilistic generators with deterministic validators and bounded repair loops to form operational floor‑safety nets. Despite many demonstrations and architectural proposals, preregistered empirical measurements that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics remain scarce.

We implemented and preregistered a narrowly scoped paired experiment to evaluate the incremental effect of a minimal guarded pipeline composed of: (1) a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), (2) a frozen deterministic validator performing canonicalization and explicit rule/dependency checks, and (3) at most one automated repair attempt when the validator reports violations. The central research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under the preregistered paired design and fixed repair budget? Our contributions are (i) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archived per‑task artifacts, (ii) confirmatory and descriptive statistics computed from those artifacts, (iii) an artifact‑grounded sensitivity bound tied to the observed discordant counts, and (iv) concrete, artifact‑traceable design recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: Recent system demonstrations and surveys document progress in intent→configuration synthesis but also document systematic LLM failure modes (omission, ordering errors, hallucination) that threaten operational safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) provide empirical evidence that verifier‑assisted pipelines and retrieval‑augmented architectures reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating analogous guarded architectures for NetOps [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Classic deterministic network verification methods (e.g., header‑space analysis and specification‑based checking) supply algorithmic foundations for validators capable of statically checking reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Surveys and standardization efforts emphasize auditability, provenance, and human‑oversight as open challenges when LLMs are embedded into operational pipelines [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our experiment is positioned to provide a tightly documented, preregistered measurement of the incremental effect of a bounded validator+repair floor under operationally motivated pairing semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered the complete experimental plan as cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 prior to observing outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses included: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly assumed a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 for power calculations; that numeric assumption is reproduced here because it materially affects inferential interpretation.

Design and pairing semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with a deterministic seed list of 300 tasks produced by a frozen generator. For each seed the experiment produced a single shared LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate) that served as the baseline response and as the starting point for the guarded arm's validation and possible repair. The preregistered intent of the shared‑candidate pairing was to emulate realistic remediation workflows (operators commonly edit a single plan) and to isolate the effect of deterministic validation and bounded repair on that same candidate. Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The shared‑candidate semantics increase within‑pair correlation and therefore reduce expected discordant pairs compared with independent‑draws designs; this tradeoff was explicitly encoded in the preregistration and must be considered in power planning.

Model and sampling determinism: The declared generation model was gpt-5-mini. The archived model configuration used in execution records shows the declared_model_version as "gpt-5-mini" and that the sampling temperature field was unset (temperature = null) in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA-256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Because the temperature parameter was not explicitly fixed in the archived configuration, provider default sampling behavior determines whether generation was effectively stochastic or deterministic; that sampling determinism is therefore unspecified in the archive. We disclose this explicitly because sampling determinism affects the interpretation of single‑draw shared‑candidate designs and of reproducibility when the provider's default sampling behavior is later changed.

Validator, canonicalization, scoring, and repair adapter: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized responses to a normalized configuration AST and applied encoded workflow and dependency checks derived from task payloads. Scoring used a full intent‑constraint validation rule: success required that the normalized_configuration satisfy the task's required_sequence, expected_final_state, and workflow policies. Validator traces recorded parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, and a boolean valid flag; these fields both triggered repair and served as structured diagnostics. The preregistered repair adapter was restricted to a single automated attempt per episode and received the shared candidate plus structured violation codes; its objective was minimal, targeted edits to remove reported violations. Repair outcomes were revalidated by the same deterministic validator to produce the final guarded decision.

Contamination, exclusions, and primary estimand: The preregistration specified deterministic contamination checks based on normalized‑AST equality and near‑duplicate lexical thresholds; exact duplicates would trigger deterministic replacement from a reserved seed list. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference). The preregistered primary test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) with paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistered missingness policy used a 'complete_pair_primary' treatment (drop pairs only if both calls failed) and allowed a single retry for provider/infrastructure failures.

Reproducibility: All deterministic seeds, task generator settings, validator trace formats, repair prompt templates, analysis code, and execution manifest were archived. Key archived artifacts cited in this manuscript include the preregistration record (preregistration SHA‑256 archived in the execution manifest), execution/model_configuration.json (SHA-256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa) documenting declared model and unset temperature, and the paired contingency artifact (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) used for confirmatory inference.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and artifact‑derived counts: Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair invocation). No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; no deterministic contamination exclusions were required.

Primary outcome counts (archived): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency (guarded vs baseline) from the archived analysis artifact analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Inferential results (preregistered procedures applied to archived artifacts): Exact McNemar two‑sided test on the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. The absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = (n10 − n01)/N = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output; the conditional repair success is 1/1 with Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]. These numeric outputs are reproduced exactly from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Why p = 1.00 occurs here (artifact‑grounded interpretation): The exact McNemar test conditions on the observed discordant total (n10 + n01 = 1) and evaluates whether the two discordant cells are symmetric under the null. With only a single discordant pair the test's reference distribution has minimal informative mass; for our observed n10=1, n01=0 the exact two‑sided McNemar p equals 1.00, reflecting that the observed single discordant pair is not extreme under the conditional null. The paired bootstrap CI and the absolute paired difference provide the more directly interpretable numerical summaries of effect magnitude in this low‑discordance regime. Analysts can reproduce these artifacts using the archived paired_contingency_table.csv and the reported bootstrap parameters (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729).

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to observed discordance: The observed discordant total (1) imposes a hard limit on resolvable absolute paired difference = 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. The preregistered target for H1 (≥50% relative reduction from a planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) implied a required absolute change on the order of 0.30, i.e., ∼90 net discordant pairs in a sample of 300. The observed near‑ceiling baseline removed statistical headroom and therefore rendered the preregistered large‑effect H1 untestable on the observed data; this fact is reported both in Methods and here in Results to make the limitation explicit and artifact‑traceable.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation and practical lessons. The archived contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0) directly constrains inferential outcomes: the absolute paired difference equals 1/300 and the exact McNemar test conditions on the single discordant pair, producing p = 1.00. That the guarded pipeline corrected the sole invalid baseline output shows that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded repair adapter can, in at least one case, remediate an invalid candidate without human intervention; however, the rarity of initial failures in our synthetic task bank means the pipeline's marginal effect on first‑pass validity is necessarily small in absolute terms on this sample.

Implications for study design and power planning. Two design levers determine the number of informative discordant pairs for paired generate→verify→repair experiments: (a) baseline failure prevalence (driven by task difficulty or adversarial augmentation) and (b) pairing semantics (shared candidate vs independent draws). Shared‑candidate pairing increases ecological validity for remediation workflows but reduces discordant counts; therefore future confirmatory studies should explicitly link pairing semantics to the estimand and calibrate task difficulty (or adversarially augment tasks) to produce a preregistered target discordant count aligned with the planned absolute/relative effect size. When repair effectiveness is a primary claim, power calculations should target the expected number of initial failures so that conditional repair success can be estimated precisely.

Construct validity, runtime semantics, and validator coverage. Our validator performed deterministic static checks and canonicalization rather than executing configurations in devices or emulators; this design avoids live changes but does not measure runtime consequences (control‑plane convergence, transient reachability). If operational deployment claims require runtime guarantees, future studies should integrate emulation or simulation stages and preregister how emulator outputs map to success/failure. The archived validator traces (violation_codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count) are central to diagnosing failure modes and should be part of any reproducible pipeline.

Limitations tied to artifacts. The principal limitation for the confirmatory H1 is empirical: the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed baseline (299/300), which removed statistical headroom for a large relative reduction; we therefore refrain from claiming confirmatory support for H1. Additional limitations (single model family, synthetic task bank, deterministic static validator, sampling determinism unspecified) restrict external generality and are discussed below with explicit artifact pointers to enable independent reanalysis.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment comparing single‑shot LLM generation (declared gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline consisting of a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair iteration. Observed results were baseline 299/300 valid and guarded 300/300 valid; the one repaired case demonstrates that automated repair can remediate some invalid candidates, but the observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and removed statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction (H1). We therefore present artifact‑grounded descriptive and conditional inference (paired counts, exact McNemar p, bootstrap CI) and offer concrete design recommendations—calibrating task difficulty, preregistering pairing semantics and repair budgets, and integrating emulation when runtime semantics matter—each traceable to archived artifacts in the execution manifest. The archived execution and analysis artifacts are the authoritative source for the numeric counts and intervals reported here.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single declared LLM (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction (H1), making that preregistered large‑effect hypothesis untestable on the observed data.

Sampling determinism is unspecified in the archived model configuration (execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null); provider default sampling behavior therefore determines whether generation was stochastic or effectively deterministic, which affects reproducibility and interpretation of single‑draw experiments.

Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference compared with independent‑draws designs.

Validation used deterministic static canonicalization and constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects (control‑plane convergence, transient reachability); runtime consequences were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 (repair success) evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
